extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of natural philosophy/scientific method; readers of Bacon's Novum Organum
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for conducting natural-philosophical inquiry per Francis Bacon: how to discover forms, construct reliable experimental methods, and investigate latent processes rather than rely on à priori or merely syllogistic reasoning. Emphasizes practical, generalizable axioms and attention to small causes and sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for experimental over à priori methods
rubrics_metrics.description: The text repeatedly endorses the experimental method and criticizes the à priori/deductive approach when applied improperly to physical inquiry (e.g., Gilbert asserting advantages of the experimental over the à priori method).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use experiment and observation as the primary route to knowledge in physical sciences; avoid relying on purely geometrical or à priori axioms to investigate natural phenomena. Example: Gilbert's De Magnete as success of experiment; anti-pattern: building natural theories from pure deduction without empirical grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspect evidence consonant to our inclinations
rubrics_metrics.description: One must 'suspect that kind of evidence which is most consonant to our inclinations, and not to admit any notion as real except we can base it firmly upon that kind of demonstration which is peculiar to the subject, not to our impression.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to confirmation bias: do not accept hypotheses because they please us. Admit claims only when supported by demonstrations appropriate to the subject. Methods that happen to align with the investigator's preferences are acceptable only if they truly fit the object (examples: Pythagoras and Descartes when methods fit the subject). Avoid constructing moral or theological systems by induction alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: True knowledge is deduction from causes; prioritize discovery of form
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘True knowledge is that which is deduced from causes.’ Of the four causes (matter, form, efficient, and end) the discovery of form is the central aim; final causes tend to corrupt natural science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus inquiry on discovering the form (the law or true difference) underlying a nature, rather than stopping at material/efficient descriptions or speculating about final causes. Treat final causes as largely irrelevant to natural science except in human affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods should be certain, free, and preparatory (practical rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘We will lay this down ... that it should be certain, free and preparatory, or having relation to practice.’ A genuine practical precept should not fail, should not confine the operator to peculiar means, and should be more practicable than the effect itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design methods that (1) reliably produce the effect, (2) are adaptable and do not require unattainable or highly specific means, and (3) are approachable in difficulty (not more difficult than the effect). Anti-pattern: prescriptive recipes that only work with rare inputs or are as hard as the target effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for discovery of forms (generalizable laws) rather than only particular causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowing the cause of a nature in particular subjects only is imperfect; discovery of forms (unifying principles present across subjects) yields genuine theory and free practice and enables production of novel effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek principles that are present whenever the nature is present and absent when it is absent; a form should be convertible with the given nature and deducible from a more known substratum. Emphasize generalizability: forms allow transfer of power across different substrates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize primary axioms from simple natures for radical operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary axioms regard the body as an aggregate of simple natures (e.g., yellowness, weight, ductility). These axioms, derived from simple natures, open broad paths to human power and radical operation on nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive and master the forms and methods for producing simple natures and their degrees; then combine them to engineer complex bodies. This primary approach yields deeper, more universal authority than piecemeal manipulation of concretes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use secondary method of investigating latent processes in concrete bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: A second axiom type proceeds by studying concrete bodies and the latent, uninterrupted processes from elements to finished forms (e.g., formation of metals, plant growth, nutritive processes, animal motion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ sequence- and process-focused studies to map the continuous series of changes in natural generation. This approach is often more prompt and practical for particular problems (and necessary where direct manipulation is impossible), but is subordinate to primary axioms for deepest understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate minute, continuous processes and smallest causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Latent processes are often subtle and escape the senses; inquiry must determine what is lost, remains, added, diluted, contracted, united, separated, continuous, or broken off, and similar fine-grained circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay attention to the smallest efforts and incremental changes—these often produce natural acts. Design experiments and observations to detect minute, continuous influences rather than only gross, obvious factors. Anti-pattern: ignoring microscale causes because they are not immediately perceptible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not place inductive and deductive methods in radical opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: The text argues there is no fundamental opposition between induction and deduction; Baconian method assumes uniformity (suppressed premise) and exemplifies syllogistic reasoning in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat induction and deduction as complementary tools within a single system: induction to discover axioms and laws from particulars, deduction to derive consequences and structure arguments. Avoid ideological rejection of one method by proponents of the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid simple enumeration (enumerationem per simplicem) as sole inductive procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Enumeration per simplicem—mere listing without regard to the nature of the matter or completeness of species—was warned against; Aristotle and Bacon both cautioned that such enumeration is a source of error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer general laws merely by counting occurrences; ensure that induction attends to the nature of the subject, completeness of cases, and the relevant distinctions among species. Use rigorous sampling and attention to underlying differences rather than naked enumeration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious with analogical illustrations and metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogies (e.g., levity vs worthlessness) can be misleading; changing terms (levity → buoyancy) may invert the argument and reveal flaw.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use analogies only when the analogy maps relevant causal or formal relations, not mere verbal resemblances. Test analogical inferences against observation and experiment; avoid overreliance on eloquent but shallow figures of speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mathematics appropriately: powerful but not a cure-all
rubrics_metrics.description: The text notes both the utility and the abuse of mathematics: Bacon censures the Pythagorean abuse (building the world from arithmetic) but acknowledges mathematical demonstration's power (Newton's work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ quantitative and mathematical methods where they genuinely illuminate relations and yield demonstrable predictions (e.g., Kepler, Newton). Avoid elevating mathematical abstractions to unwarranted ontological primacy when they lack empirical grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits of logical definitions for primordial notions
rubrics_metrics.description: Logical definitions must be given in simpler terms than the object; for primordial notions and objects of sense this is impossible, so we must often rest with mere names of perceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge when precise analytic definitions are infeasible; do not force artificial definitions for fundamental sensory concepts. Accept nominal labels when deeper, simpler primitives are not available, and proceed with careful empirical description.
